name: Freemasonry
notes: Many independent jurisdictions; rituals vary by jurisdiction and period.

name: Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn
notes: Original order fragmented after 1900; several modern successor orders claim the name.

name: Ordo Templi Orientis
notes: Several competing organizations use the name.

name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
notes: Temple ceremonies are described by the church as sacred rather than secret.

name: Druze
notes: Divided into initiated (ʿuqqāl) and uninitiated (juhhāl) members.

name: Transcendental Meditation
notes: Presents itself as a non-religious technique; its religious status is disputed. In Malnak v. Yogi (1977–1979) US federal courts held that its school course was religious in nature.

name: Tibetan Buddhism (Vajrayana)
notes: Tantric practice is organised by lineages of the Nyingma, Kagyu, Sakya and Gelug schools.

name: Shingon Buddhism
notes: Main centres at Mount Kōya and Tō-ji.

name: Śākta Tantra (Kaula and Śrīvidyā)
notes: Goddess-centred tantric lineages; the Wikidata item is for Shaktism as a whole.

name: Naqshbandi order
notes: Sunni Sufi order with many branches, including the Mujaddidi and Khalidi lines.

name: Bektashi Order
notes: Banned in Turkey with all Sufi orders in 1925; the world headquarters moved to Tirana.

name: Eleusinian Mysteries
notes: Ended at the close of the 4th century CE.

name: Mithraic Mysteries
notes: No internal text explaining the cult survives.

name: Hopi religion
notes: Ceremonies are held by clans and religious societies in the Hopi villages. Wikidata has an item for the Hopi people (Q117255) but not for the religion.

name: Ngarrindjeri religion
region: Lower Murray and Coorong, South Australia
notes: Wikidata has an item for the Ngarrindjeri people (Q370543) but not for the religion.

name: Heaven and Earth Society (Tiandihui, Hung League)
founded: 18th century (its legend places the founding under the Kangxi emperor)
notes: Sworn brotherhood with initiation rites, oaths and recognition signs. Later Hung lodges and the triads claim descent from it.

name: Daoism
notes: Scriptures, talismans and methods were transmitted from master to disciple under covenant (CLM-0048, CLM-0049).

name: Alawites (Nusayris)
notes: The religion is taught to men through a staged initiation (CLM-0054).

name: Brahmanical (Vedic) tradition
notes: The tradition of Vedic recitation and the rites of the twice-born as laid down in the Dharmaśāstras.

name: Shugendō
notes: Mountain asceticism combining esoteric Buddhism with Japanese kami worship; major centres at Ōmine, Kumano and Haguro.

name: Arrernte religion
notes: Also spelled Aranda. Ceremonies, songs and sacred objects (tjurunga) are held by men and women of the relevant estates and degree of initiation.

name: Pitjantjatjara religion
region: Western Desert (north-west South Australia, south-west Northern Territory, eastern Western Australia)
notes: Also spelled Pitjantjara. Shares much restricted knowledge with neighbouring Western Desert peoples.

name: Midewiwin (Grand Medicine Society)
region: Great Lakes and upper Mississippi (Ojibwe and neighbouring Anishinaabe peoples)
notes: A graded medicine society of Mide' priests, entered by initiation and payment; its songs and teachings are recorded on birch-bark scrolls.

name: Kwakwaka'wakw religion
region: Northern Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland coast (British Columbia)
notes: Older literature calls the people Kwakiutl. The winter ceremonial is organised in dancing societies led by the hamatsa (Wikidata Q5644160 for the hamatsa). Wikidata has no item for the religion.

name: Sámi religion (noaidi practice)
region: Sápmi (northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola Peninsula)
notes: Ritual specialists (noaidi) used the drum (goavddis, runebomme) for divination and healing. The practice was prosecuted as witchcraft by Danish-Norwegian and Swedish authorities in the 17th and 18th centuries (CLM-0087).

name: Mazatec mushroom religion
founded: pre-Columbian (mushroom rites); blended with Catholicism after the conquest
region: Sierra Mazateca (Huautla de Jiménez and neighbouring towns), Oaxaca, Mexico
notes: Healers (curanderos, sabios) hold night vigils with psilocybin mushrooms, which they call the saint children. Wikidata has items for the Mazatec people (Q1262708) and for María Sabina (Q442467) but not for the religion.

name: Sande societies in Liberia
notes: Spiritual and cultural initiation associations. Membership may coexist with Christianity or Islam. The records below concern the places and reporting periods in the cited sources, not all members or all Liberian traditions.

name: Poro societies in Liberia
notes: Spiritual and cultural initiation associations. Keep distinct from Sande and from the separate societies discussed in ritual-murder allegations; the source does not equate them.

name: NXIVM and DOS
region: United States; cases examined in New York
notes: A self-described coaching movement and an inner secret society. Included for initiatory secrecy and concealed governance; this classification does not establish religious status.

name: Oghar/Aghori practitioners in Moti Nath’s account
notes: A narrowly attributed historical account, not a classification of all Aghori lineages.

name: Cherokee practitioners in Mooney’s North Carolina collection
region: Cherokee reservation, North Carolina, United States
notes: Scope is the named practitioners and manuscripts collected in 1887–1888; not every Cherokee community or present-day practice.

name: Chaui Pawnee Hako in Tahirussawichi’s account
region: Pawnee communities in Oklahoma, United States
notes: Chaui version documented with ritual keeper Tahirussawichi and Pawnee collaborator James R. Murie. Ceremonial Father and Son are roles, not a description of all family relationships.

name: Osage child-naming ritual specialists
notes: The source distinguishes gentes, versions and rights to transmit particular recitations; it does not describe one uniform entitlement to all Osage knowledge.

name: Selk’nam Hain in the accounts collected by Anne Chapman
region: Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego, Argentina and Chile
notes: Historical rites, recollections and recorded songs. The dated sources do not establish the absence of living Selk’nam descendants or the status of present-day practice.

name: Barasana He House initiation
notes: Specific account discussed by Bonnemère from Stephen Hugh-Jones’s fieldwork. Kawillary comparisons are not assigned to the Barasana.

name: Iglulingmiut and Aivilingmiut angakkuq training in Rasmussen’s account
region: Igloolik and Aivilik areas, eastern Canadian Arctic
notes: Scope follows the report’s named interlocutors and communities, not all Inuit traditions. Historical titles retain the publisher’s terminology; catalogue descriptions use specific community names.

name: Long Valley Patwin initiation in Loeb’s historical account
region: Long Valley, northern California, United States
notes: Local historical versions recounted to Loeb in 1931, not a claim about all Patwin communities or present-day practice. Loeb names Wilson Lewis and his wife as the Long Valley interlocutors.

name: Sambia male initiation in Gilbert Herdt’s field accounts
notes: Name and scope follow Herdt’s accounts. Neighbouring Anga peoples and later generations are not assigned the same practices. The later chapter explicitly limits its ethnography to 1993 and notes subsequent radical change.

name: Gardnerian Wicca in the exposed Book of Shadows recension
region: British-origin ritual texts; later exposed web compilation
notes: Scope is the exposed recension attributed to Gardner, not every coven or all Wicca. Editorial date estimates and Internet-copy history do not authenticate an ancient origin or present-day uniformity.

name: Zuni initiatory fraternities in Stevenson’s account
region: Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico, United States
notes: Scope is selected historical initiations, with Ko’tikili and Wood-fraternity rites recorded separately. Neither all Zuni ritual nor present-day practice is represented. The source identifies observations and reports unevenly; those distinctions remain attached.

name: Munduruku karoko custodianship in Murphy’s field account
region: Savannah villages of the upper Tapajós region, Pará, Brazil
notes: Selected 1952–1953 field material, especially Cabruá and Cabitutú. Not all Munduruku communities or present-day transmission rules.

name: Abakuá initiation in Lydia Cabrera’s collected accounts
region: Cuba; accounts include Matanzas, Havana-area communities and Cárdenas
notes: A religious confraternity with local Potencias and differentiated ranks. Cabrera combines testimony and variants; publication in 1969 does not date every reported event. Not a uniform rule for every Abakuá community.

name: Cuban Osha-Ifá in the Proyecto Orunmila Atefá compilation
region: Regla and Guanabacoa collection context, Havana, Cuba; diaspora web circulation
notes: The inspected source presents a practitioner compilation and acknowledges variation among religious branches. It does not represent every Cuban or West African Ifá lineage. Its stated manuscript-comparison process has not been independently audited.
